The budget strips rights from citizens and was pushed through fast, without public consultation.

The Constitutional Court did strike a labour-law transitional provision from the budget (Decision 17 of 20 October 2026), which supports the 'rights' half. The 'fast track, no consultation' half was not independently established here; the cabinet published a summary on 14 October 2026.
The Constitutional Court held a week ago that this budget is not unconstitutional.

The Court ruled on 20 October 2026, nine days before the debate. It annulled two provisions on procedural grounds but left the budget in force, so 'not unconstitutional' captures the outcome while omitting the partial annulment.
The Court annulled two provisions of a technical character that will most likely be corrected.
Decision 17 of 20 October 2026 annulled two provisions, and the Court's reasoning was that the labour-code change was not tied to the budget's revenues and expenditures - i.e. a procedural defect.
The budget cuts the labour rights of Bulgarian citizens.

From 1 January 2027 length of service was to be counted by actual hours worked, so a permanent half-time worker would accrue ten days of paid leave instead of twenty. The provision was struck down, but it was in the bill.
The assertion that the budget cuts labour rights is not true.
The bill contained a provision that halved paid-leave accrual for part-time workers; that is a cut to a labour right, and the Constitutional Court later removed it.
Denies the content of a provision that existed.
The disputed matter is one text on holidays and hourly work.
The contested transitional provision concerned counting length of service by hours worked, which affects holidays and hourly employment.
The Court's objection was that this must be done, if at all, by amending another law.
The Court held the amendment was not directly tied to the budget's revenues and expenditures, so it could not be carried by the budget law's transitional provisions.
Rights are being stolen from part-time workers, working students and young mothers.
The struck provision would have reduced leave accrual for exactly those groups; the characterisation is rhetorical but the incidence is documented.
The budget adds about 2 billion euro of administrative and tax burden on business and households.

168 chasa, working from the plan sent to the European Commission, reports 'nearly EUR 2 billion' of additional revenue and itemises it, including an EUR 800 m one-off windfall tax. Sega puts the total effect of new measures at EUR 988 m. The cabinet denies 'new taxes' altogether. The figure is defensible on one reading and roughly double another.
The dispute is partly definitional: revenue measures versus net burden.
A further 1.5 billion euro is allocated against empty line items.
The bTV recap records the claim but no primary document was located showing which line items are unfunded.
About one million pensioners will remain below the poverty line.
NSI data for end-June 2026 put about 750,000 pensioners below the poverty line, against a 2027 line of EUR 443. The rounded 'one million' overstates by roughly a third.
At the end there was no money even for salaries.

The fiscal reserve stood at EUR 6.8 bn at 30 April 2026; salaries and pensions are first in the priority order of the extended budget law, and post-debate fact-checking refuted the claim on Finance Ministry figures.
A false claim about a documented figure.
Gyurov's proposal was to take money from the Bulgarian Development Bank.
On 22 April 2026 the caretaker cabinet authorised the finance minister, as sole shareholder, to reduce BBR's capital; the stated purpose was to return money to the budget.
BBR itself warned the reduction would take months and needed creditor approval.
The fiscal reserve held 6.8 billion euro, so paying salaries was never the question.
The finance minister put the reserve at EUR 6.8 bn on 30 April 2026 - EUR 5.3 bn of deposits plus EUR 1.5 bn of EU receivables.
Gyurov said then that he had an acute shortage of money, while now saying the funds were not needed for salaries.
The record shows a dispute about liquidity timing rather than an admission of insolvency. The 'acute shortage' quotation could not be matched to a primary source.
The new government inherited not a zero budget but one at nearly minus 3 billion.
Finance Ministry data put the consolidated deficit at end-April 2026 at a figure far below EUR 3 bn, and post-debate fact-checking rated this claim false.
The single clearest false number in the debate.
Gyurov's government left 6.8 billion to the next government.
Same figure as C-05-34: EUR 6.8 bn on 30 April 2026, immediately before the government change on 8 May.
She submitted all documents on the pardon to the prosecution under her own signature.
The presidency referred the Atanasov case to the prosecution on 19 October 2026 and sent the entire file.
The decision was taken entirely on humanitarian and health grounds.

The presidency asserts a statutory procedure and a humanitarian case; the medical commission's actual recommendation was contested, and one report says the proposal came from the Pardon Commission instead.
All attempts to obtain information and hold a hearing on the topic were prevented by Progressive Bulgaria.
No record of the specific procedural blocking was located.
Would need the committee's agenda and voting record.
Only two people on that medical commission were replaced.
The presidency released only pseudonymised initials, so the turnover could not be verified.
The commission's composition documents before and after the replacements.
There is a separate commission that deals with pardons.
The Pardon Commission is a distinct advisory body; the medical commission is a separate statutory body under the penal sanctions act.
No document has been shown in which the medical commission states that this person should be pardoned.
The register is public but, per the presidency's own first defence, omits part of the case file; the medical commission's recommendation was not published at the time of the debate.
The commission is not appointed at the minister's discretion; it exists under the law.
For the medical commission this is correct: it is a seven-member body with a three-year mandate under the Execution of Penal Sanctions Act.
The Pardon Commission, by contrast, exists by presidential decree - a distinction the debate blurred.
Its documents bear the signatures of at least three ministers.
The presidency asserts ministerial signatures on the file; the documents themselves were not published in full.
Fourteen inquiries were sent to her administration and fourteen answers were received.
No register of the inquiries was located.
When Bulgaria stood aside with a veto, the whole European Union was against it.

Bulgaria blocked North Macedonia's accession in 2020 and lifted the veto on 24 June 2022 by adopting the French presidency proposal. That other member states opposed the veto is documented in outline but 'the whole EU' is an overstatement.
The French proposal changed the question from Bulgaria versus the EU to North Macedonia versus the EU.

The 47th Assembly's decision of 24 June 2022 attached conditions to the French proposal, and the EU opened accession talks with North Macedonia on 19 July 2022 - the framework did shift the dispute into the accession process.
This placed Bulgaria in a much stronger position than a veto would have.
An evaluative judgement about negotiating leverage; the procedural facts are documented, the comparison is not testable.
She spoke before the leaders of 193 states.
Iotova addressed the general debate of the 81st UN General Assembly on 23 September 2026; the Assembly has 193 member states.
Technically the audience is the Assembly, not 193 heads of state.
The UN resolution itself provided for a cessation of military operations.
On 24 February 2026 the General Assembly adopted a resolution calling for an immediate, full and unconditional ceasefire.
Our position was initially one of support.
Bulgaria voted in favour of the 24 February 2026 resolution, alongside Germany, France, Italy and others.
There is no UN General Assembly resolution.
A resolution was adopted on 24 February 2026; Bulgaria voted for it.
Denies the existence of a document she voted for.
In the statement he means, Bulgaria's national interest and the Black Sea could not have been protected.
This is an evaluative claim about a September 2026 joint declaration; it is not falsifiable from the record.
The text of the September 2026 joint declaration.
She does not recall Bulgaria ever imposing a veto on anything.
Bulgaria imposed a veto on North Macedonia's EU accession in 2020 and lifted it on 24 June 2022.
A memory claim, but contradicted by the record she was discussing.
Bulgaria took part in drafting all documents in every format it participates in.
Council of the EU drafting records for the relevant formats.
A huge mass of votes has been lost between the parliamentary elections and now.
Progressive Bulgaria won 1,444,924 votes on 19 April 2026; Iotova took 528,951 on 25 October - a fall of roughly 900,000.
The arithmetic from the two official results is about 916,000; the '900,000' figure was put into circulation by Alpha Research on election night and is accurate as an approximation.
Polling agencies showed a 20% gap, but the actual difference was under 3%.
Gallup International Balkan's September-October survey gave Iotova a lead of at least 20 points; the first round ended 34.759% to 31.952%, a gap of 2.807 points.
The Consultative Council was convened too late, after weeks of indication of escalation.
It was convened on 7 October 2026, the day after two merchant ships were hit; whether that was 'too late' depends on what was known beforehand.
The Council produced no concrete decisions or goals.
The 7 October 2026 KSNC published an opinion and concrete proposals condemning the strikes and setting out measures.
